"Virtually" means: so close to something that the remaining gap doesn't matter in practice.

Think of a scale from 0 to 100. Something that is "virtually complete" sits at 97 or 98 — not quite 100, but so close that for all real-world purposes, you can treat it as 100. The key isn't just the closeness — it's the judgment that the gap is small enough to ignore.

This one idea — close enough that the difference is negligible — is the heart of "virtually."

"Virtually" works in two related ways.

Sense 1: Almost / Nearly

This is the most common modern use. "Virtually" here means "almost entirely" or "as good as."

  • "The earthquake virtually destroyed the city."
    → The city was almost completely destroyed. Some parts may have survived, but the damage is so total that you can treat it as destroyed.
  • "Virtually everyone agrees the Earth is round."
    → Maybe a tiny number of people disagree, but that number is so small it barely counts.
  • "She has virtually no money left."
    → She might have a few coins, but practically speaking, she's broke.

In this sense, "virtually" tells you: the full statement is not 100% true, but it's so close to 100% that the leftover exception is barely worth mentioning.

Sense 2: In effect / Essentially

Here, "virtually" means something functions as or has the same effect as the thing named — even if technically or officially it isn't that thing.

  • "He is virtually the boss."
    → He doesn't have the title of boss, but he behaves like one and everyone treats him like one. In terms of real-world effect, he is the boss.
  • "By refusing to speak, she virtually admitted she was guilty."
    → She didn't technically say "I'm guilty," but her silence had the same effect as an admission.
  • "These two products are virtually identical."
    → They're not exactly the same down to every detail, but the differences are so minor that for any practical purpose, they're the same thing.

In this sense, "virtually" tells you: this may not be the official or technical truth, but in terms of what actually happens or what it means in reality, it's effectively the same.

These aren't really two separate meanings — they're two faces of the same coin. Both are saying: the gap between reality and the stated thing is so small or unimportant that we can ignore it.

  • In Sense 1, you're ignoring a gap of degree: "almost all" → "all."
  • In Sense 2, you're ignoring a gap of category: "not officially X" → "but effectively X."

The judgment in both cases is the same: the gap doesn't change anything in practice.

"Almost" and "nearly" simply point to a gap: not quite there yet. They're neutral about whether the gap matters.

"Virtually" goes one step further: it says the gap doesn't matter. It carries a judgment — "close enough."

Compare:

  • "He almost finished the project."
    → He's not done; he still has real work left. The sentence is neutral — it doesn't tell us how significant the remaining work is.
  • "He virtually finished the project."
    → He's as good as done. The remaining work is so small you could treat the project as finished.

Another pair:

  • "She almost cried."
    → She was close to crying, but held back.
  • "She virtually cried."
    → She was so visibly overwhelmed that the line between crying and not-crying barely applies — it was essentially crying.

This is "virtually" at its most precise: it doesn't just describe how close something is — it makes a judgment about that closeness: "close enough to treat as the real thing."

• "The company virtually dominates the market."
    → It doesn't have 100% market share, but its share is so dominant that it controls the market in every meaningful way.
  • "It is virtually impossible to fake this test."
    → Maybe one person in a million could do it. But practically, you can consider it impossible.
  • "He virtually grew up in that library."
    → He didn't literally live there, but he spent so much time there that in effect, that's where he was shaped and raised.
  • "Virtually nothing has changed."
    → There might be the tiniest difference, but nothing meaningful.
  • "She virtually runs the team, even though the title belongs to someone else."
    → In terms of actual function and influence, she is the team leader.

"Virtually" is especially powerful when used with words like no, nothing, nobody, impossible, unknown — to say something is so rare or absent that it barely exists:

  • "There is virtually no evidence." → There might be a trace, but nothing that counts.
  • "Virtually nobody showed up." → Maybe one or two people, but not enough to be significant.
  • "He virtually never makes mistakes." → Extremely rare — almost never.
  • "The side effects are virtually undetectable." → They might exist in theory, but you'd never notice them.

In these uses, "virtually" is doing something clever: it acknowledges that the exception technically exists while insisting it's too small to change the conclusion.
A Usage Caution: The Modern Technology Sense

In casual modern speech, particularly around remote work, you'll hear things like:

  • "We met virtually." (= we met over video call)
  • "The event will be held virtually." (= online, not in person)

This is a newer, separate usage tied to the idea of a "virtual" digital space. It doesn't mean "almost met" or "essentially met" — it simply means the meeting happened through a screen. This use is now extremely common and you'll encounter it often.

Just know: this is a different use from everything explained above. Context will always make it clear which meaning is intended.
"Virtually" means: so nearly or effectively [something] that any remaining gap is too small or irrelevant to matter in practice.
